notes:
I've grouped these notes verse by verse, and every point has its URL. A few gaps first:

- **Enduring Word cut off at v. 13.** For vv. 13–17 I relied mainly on the Pulpit Commentary, Wesley's Notes and the Expositor's Bible.
- **Gill and Calvin** turned up only for vv. 1 and 12. Spurgeon's main exposition page wouldn't load; his comments here come from search excerpts and quotations in other sources.
- **Not found at all:** NET Bible notes, Orthodox (oca.org) material, Lutheran or Pentecostal sources, and anything on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this psalm. Those are left out.
- **No real denominational disagreement.** The sources I found don't show Protestant traditions splitting over this psalm. The differences below are about how to translate or apply individual verses. I've labelled each source's tradition so you can compare them.

---

**Title / authorship**
- Traditional view: Enduring Word says this *prayer of Moses* was almost certainly written during the wilderness years on the way to Canaan. It links the psalm to Numbers 20, citing Boice: Miriam's death, Moses striking the rock, and Aaron's death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-90/
- GotQuestions calls it the oldest psalm, written by Moses by the year 1440 BC. https://www.gotquestions.org/prayer-of-Moses.html
- Spurgeon (Baptist) says to read the whole Psalm as written for the tribes in the desert. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps090.cfm
- Critical view (Ellicott): Ellicott thinks the Mosaic title was probably a vague tradition. He says the contrast between human frailty and God's unchanging nature is more suited to a later age of Israel than an early one, and that the "How long?" of v. 13 even suggests the Maccabean age. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-90.html
- Utley (bible.org) says the psalm titles are ancient Jewish traditions but not originally part of the inspired text. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-90
- A note on StudyLight's v. 1 page dates the psalm to the time of or after the exile. It suggests the "work of our hands" (v. 17) could be the rebuilding of the temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/90-1.html
- Catholic (Augustine): Augustine doubted Moses wrote all of it. He thought Moses' name was used to point readers to something. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801090.htm

**v. 1**
- Guzik: more than their tents or armies, Israel had God as their refuge. God's care began with Abraham, not with the exodus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-90/
- Spurgeon pictures Moses saying that even as wanderers in the desert we find a home in thee. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps090.cfm
- Translation: Ellicott notes that the Greek (LXX) and Latin (Vulgate) have "refuge", probably from a slightly different Hebrew word. He still prefers "abode", because a lasting home is the psalm's key idea. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-90.html
- Reformed (Calvin): God setting Abraham's descendants apart shows the grace of adoption. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/90-1.html
- Baptist (Gill): Gill reads "refuge" in terms of Christ, the fulfilment of the cities of refuge. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/90-1.html
- A writer quoted in Spurgeon's Treasury of David says this opening points to a certain hope of the resurrection and of eternal life: God is life, so those who live in him live. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-90.html
- Catholic (Augustine): Augustine reads "generations" as perhaps two, the old and the new, since Moses served the Old Covenant and foretold the New. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801090.htm

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: "from everlasting to everlasting" literally means from hidden time to hidden. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-90.html
- Spurgeon: if God could change, he would be an unreliable refuge. God's eternity is stated to show, by contrast, how short human life is. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps090.cfm
- Methodist (Wesley): God has had all his perfections from eternity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/90.htm
- Catholic (Augustine): Augustine links this to God's name "I Am" (Exodus 3:14). He calls God's eternity the refuge we flee to from a world where everything changes. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801090.htm

**v. 3**
- Main view (Guzik): "Return" is not a call to repent. It is God's command that man go back to dust, echoing the curse of Genesis 3:19. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-90/
- Methodist (Wesley) agrees, adding that man was made happy and immortal but made mortal because of sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/90.htm
- Alternative view: the Pulpit Commentary reads "Return" as "come back and fill the earth again". It may refer to the Flood and the re-peopling of the earth, or to one generation constantly replacing another. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/90.htm
- Ellicott reads it the same way, as generations succeeding each other. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-90.html
- Catholic (Augustine), following the Latin text: Augustine reads it as a prayer, "Turn not man to lowness", meaning don't let us drift into craving earthly things. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801090.htm

**v. 4**
- Pulpit: time doesn't exist for God, so we shouldn't judge his ways by our own. It links the verse to 2 Peter 3:8. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/90.htm
- Ellicott warns against using the verse for Millennarian computations (end-times date-setting). It simply contrasts God's eternity with our short lives. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-90.html
- Wesley: a night watch lasted three or four hours. Time feels long ahead of us but short once it's past. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/90.htm
- Utley (bible.org) suggests "a thousand years" may recall the people before the Flood, who lived nearly that long. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-90-eternal-god-ephemeral-man
- Desiring God: if God sees a thousand years like yesterday, then the longest human lives don't span even two hours of yesterday. That doesn't make us unimportant, because God measures significance by what he values, not by length of time. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/life-is-too-brief-to-waste

**vv. 5–6**
- Pulpit: in "they are as a sleep", life is like a dream, vague and soon forgotten. The grass image echoes Isaiah 40:7 and James 1:10–11. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/90.htm
- Wesley: God sweeps away all mankind without exception, and life is as short and empty as sleep. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/90.htm
- Translation (Ellicott): Ellicott proposes a slightly re-pointed Hebrew text that gives the image of time itself carrying people away like a flood. He says the LXX and Vulgate partly support this. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-90.html

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: here the psalmist turns from mankind in general to his own people's sin. The wording fits the wilderness, when the guilty generation was slowly dying off. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/90.htm
- Ellicott: the switch to "we" makes it a lament over Israel's lost glory. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-90.html
- TGC (Themelios): the anger here is not an occasional outburst. It is God's righteous judgment, which shows itself in our mortality and short lives (Romans 1:18). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/numbering-and-being-glad-in-our-days-a-meditation-on-psalm-90/
- Catholic (Augustine): our mortality is a punishment for sin. We waste away and are troubled by the fear of death. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801090.htm

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: instead of overlooking their sins, God has set them in the searching light of his holiness, including sins they didn't know about (compare Psalm 19:12). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/90.htm
- Ellicott and the Expositor's Bible: the word for "light" here is not the usual one in "light of your face" (which normally means favour). It means a light-giving body, like the sun, that exposes everything. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-90.html ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-90.html
- Wesley: God watches as a righteous judge and has brought hidden sins to light through his judgments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/90.htm

**v. 9**
- Pulpit and Ellicott: "a tale that is told" (KJV) is better translated "a murmur" or "a sigh". We bring our years to an end. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/90.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-90.html
- TGC: the "sigh" suggests lives that end in futility and unmet hopes. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/psalm-90-psalm-106/

**v. 10**
- Guzik: Moses himself lived to 120. "Seventy years" is a poetic estimate, not a promise or a limit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-90/
- Pulpit: "their strength" is better "their pride". People may boast of reaching old age, but it brings little real benefit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/90.htm
- Ellicott follows a slightly different reading in the LXX and Vulgate: "Yet their additional years are but labour and sorrow." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-90.html
- Wesley: "fly away" pictures life fleeing like a bird. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/90.htm
- Spurgeon's devotional reading: The mortal fades to make room for the immortal. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps090.cfm

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: who can grasp God's anger as fully as the proper fear of him requires? The verse is meant to impress how terrible his anger is. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/90.htm
- Methodist (Wesley): God's wrath matches the fear sinners have of a just God, and is in fact far greater. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/90.htm
- Spurgeon's preaching outline: the full extent of God's anger against sin is not seen in this life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-90.html
- Catholic (Augustine): Augustine treats trouble in this life as God's mercy, discipline that saves from eternal punishment. When God seems to spare a sinner, that can be the heavier anger. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801090.htm

**v. 12**
- Ligonier: people often treat this as a proverb meaning "life is short, so live wisely". In the context of the whole psalm it means more. Facing our weakness honestly is the foundation of wisdom. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/teach-us-number-our-days
- Baptist (Gill): this isn't counting days or guessing how many are left. It means living each day as if it might be the last, and seeking Christ, the wisdom of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/90-12.htm
- Methodist (Wesley): consider how short life is and how surely and soon death comes, so we can give ourselves to true wisdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/90.htm
- Matthew Henry, on StudyLight's v. 12 page: this "arithmetic" must be learned from God, by his Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/90-12.html
- Alternative view (Ellicott): the verse literally makes God the one who allots our days. Its close link to v. 11 means: teach us the power of your anger, so we can offer you a wise heart. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-90.html
- GotQuestions connects it with the rich fool in Luke 12. https://www.gotquestions.org/teach-us-to-number-our-days.html

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: "turn from your anger". God isn't a man who changes his mind (Numbers 23:19), yet he relents toward his servants. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/90.htm
- Wesley: return to us in mercy, and relent from your severe dealings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/90.htm
- Catholic (Augustine): Augustine applies this to Christian martyrs suffering persecution. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801090.htm

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: "in the morning" means after a night of trouble, give a bright morning of peace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/90.htm
- Wesley takes "early" to mean "speedily". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/90.htm
- TGC: God's steadfast love "reverses everything" for people ruined by sin and judgment. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/numbering-and-being-glad-in-our-days-a-meditation-on-psalm-90/

**v. 15**
- Pulpit: let our joy last as long as our sorrow did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/90.htm
- Expositor's Bible (Maclaren): the psalmist is not thinking of any future beyond the grave; but his prayer is a prophecy, often fulfilled in this life and always afterwards. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-90.html

**v. 16**
- Pulpit: "work" and "glory" mean the same thing. If Moses wrote the psalm, the work may be settling Israel in Canaan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/90.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: "your work" means God's acts of providence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/psalms-90.html
- Maclaren: he prays that later generations will see even greater displays of God's power. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-90.html

**v. 17**
- Pulpit: "beauty" (BSB "favor") rests on us when we see how lovely God's character is. The repeated line adds emphasis, and the kind of work is not stated. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/90.htm
- Bible Hub: the Hebrew *noʿam* means delightful grace, not just physical beauty. https://biblehub.com/psalms/90.htm
- Methodist (Wesley): God's gracious influence and presence. Work not only for us but "in us". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/90.htm
- Spurgeon's Treasury (Gill citing Jewish commentators): Rashi took "the work of our hands" to mean building the tabernacle in the wilderness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-90.html
- Treasury of David: v. 16 and v. 17 pair God's work with man's work, God's power giving life to human effort. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-90.html
- Maclaren: a life touched by God's favour carries the seeds of immortality. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-90.html
